title: Endoscopy Sedation: Monitor the Airway, Not Just Comfort
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sedation for endoscopy can depress ventilation and consciousness. Monitor cardiopulmonary status and level of sedation, recognize when sedation is deeper than intended, and summon qualified rescue support promptly.
recognize: Snoring/obstructed breathing, slowed respirations, declining oxygenation, hypotension, reduced responsiveness, or unexpected deep sedation require immediate attention.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing, circulation, level of consciousness, and procedure response; activate the sedation rescue pathway when needed.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, oxygen saturation, heart rate, respiratory/ventilatory status, and sedation level per protocol.
interventions: Position/support the airway and apply ordered oxygen/ventilation assistance while calling trained rescue personnel as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Sedation medication administration and reversal are role/credential dependent; never give additional sedative solely because the patient is moving without reassessing depth and physiology.
teaching: After sedation, follow driving, supervision, and medication restrictions provided by the procedural team.
delegationScope: Endoscopy sedation roles vary by licensure, credentialing, and facility policy; PN/LVN should monitor only within approved competency and escalate deterioration.
examTrap: Giving more sedative because the patient reports discomfort despite new respiratory depression.
oneLinePearl: Sedation safety means recognizing when comfort has become physiologic compromise.
sourceBasis: ASGE Guidelines for Sedation and Anesthesia in GI Endoscopy

title: After Upper Endoscopy: Severe Pain or Crepitus Can Signal Perforation
bottomLine: Mild throat discomfort can occur after EGD, but severe chest/abdominal pain, dyspnea, fever, tachycardia, subcutaneous crepitus, rigid abdomen, or hemodynamic instability can indicate perforation and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Pain that is severe, progressive, or accompanied by systemic or respiratory findings is not routine postprocedure discomfort.
priorities: Assess ABCs, vital signs, pain location/quality, abdominal findings, and signs of free air/sepsis; notify the procedural team emergently.
assessMonitor: Trend hemodynamics, respiratory status, fever, abdominal exam, swallowing difficulty, and pain.
interventions: Keep NPO if perforation is suspected and follow emergency imaging/surgical evaluation orders.
medicationSafety: Do not repeatedly medicate severe new pain without investigating the cause.
teaching: Seek urgent care after discharge for severe pain, fever, breathing difficulty, or vomiting blood.
delegationScope: Routine recovery observation may be shared; suspected perforation requires licensed assessment and emergency escalation.
examTrap: Calling severe post-EGD chest pain expected from insufflated air.
oneLinePearl: Severe progressive pain after endoscopy is a complication cue until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: ASGE Adverse Events Associated With EGD guidance

title: Bowel Prep: Hydration, Renal Function, and Medication Safety Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Colonoscopy preparation can cause dehydration and electrolyte or medication problems, especially in frail patients or those with kidney, cardiac, or diabetes-related risks. Follow the prescribed preparation and medication plan rather than giving generic instructions.
recognize: Poor intake, vomiting, dizziness, oliguria, diabetes medications, diuretics, anticoagulants, and CKD increase preparation complexity.
priorities: Verify the exact bowel-prep, clear-liquid/fasting, and medication instructions and escalate inability to tolerate the preparation or signs of dehydration.
assessMonitor: Review hydration, comorbidities, renal risk, diabetes plan, anticoagulants, and transportation/sedation arrangements.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed fluid choices and timing; contact the procedural team for persistent vomiting or incomplete preparation.
medicationSafety: Do not independently alter insulin, anticoagulants, or other high-risk medications; individualized instructions are required.
teaching: Use the exact preparation instructions and call if vomiting or illness prevents safe completion.
delegationScope: Teaching reinforcement may be within PN/LVN role; medication adjustment decisions require authorized prescriber/procedural guidance.
examTrap: Telling every diabetic patient to skip all medications the day before colonoscopy.
oneLinePearl: Bowel prep is a medication-and-hydration plan, not just a laxative.
sourceBasis: ASGE colonoscopy and sedation safety principles

title: After Polypectomy: Delayed Bleeding Can Happen After Discharge
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Significant rectal bleeding, clots, dizziness, syncope, tachycardia, or weakness after polypectomy requires prompt evaluation. Delayed bleeding can occur even after an initially uncomplicated recovery.
recognize: Small transient spotting differs from ongoing bright-red bleeding or systemic symptoms.
priorities: Assess hemodynamics and bleeding amount, notify the procedural team, and arrange urgent evaluation for significant or symptomatic bleeding.
assessMonitor: Trend stool/bleeding, pulse/BP, dizziness, abdominal pain, and anticoagulant/antiplatelet history.
interventions: Follow post-polypectomy emergency instructions and keep patient safe from falls if symptomatic.
medicationSafety: Medication restart/hold timing for anticoagulants or antiplatelets is individualized; do not invent changes after bleeding.
teaching: Know which amount/type of bleeding requires immediate care and the medication restart plan.
delegationScope: Observation may be delegated; symptomatic bleeding requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a dizzy patient with ongoing bright-red bleeding that blood is common after polyp removal.
oneLinePearl: Delayed post-polypectomy bleeding is real—symptoms decide urgency.

title: After ERCP: New Epigastric Pain Can Mean Pancreatitis
bottomLine: New or worsening epigastric pain, persistent nausea/vomiting, tenderness, fever, or systemic deterioration after ERCP requires evaluation for post-ERCP pancreatitis and other procedure complications.
recognize: Pain extending to the back with vomiting or progressive tenderness is not routine recovery discomfort.
priorities: Assess pain, hemodynamics, hydration, abdominal findings, and ordered laboratory results; notify the endoscopy/medical team promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, nausea/vomiting, temperature, pulse/BP, abdominal exam, intake/output, and pancreatic enzymes when ordered.
interventions: Maintain prescribed NPO/fluid/analgesia plan and monitor response.
medicationSafety: Do not rely on escalating opioids alone when pain is worsening; evaluate the cause.
teaching: Seek urgent care after discharge for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, black/bloody stools, or breathing difficulty.
delegationScope: Routine recovery observations may be shared; suspected post-ERCP pancreatitis requires licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Calling severe post-ERCP abdominal pain expected because the bile duct was instrumented.
oneLinePearl: Progressive pain after ERCP is a complication signal, not a normal souvenir.
sourceBasis: ASGE ERCP adverse-event and endoscopy safety principles

title: After ERCP: Fever or Bleeding Requires Rapid Reassessment
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Fever/rigors, jaundice, hypotension, worsening RUQ pain, melena/hematemesis, or hemodynamic change after ERCP can indicate cholangitis, bleeding, or other serious complications and requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Systemic infection cues or GI bleeding after biliary intervention should not be dismissed as sedation recovery.
priorities: Assess ABCs, sepsis/bleeding findings, and notify the procedural/medical team immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, BP/HR, mental status, jaundice, abdominal pain, stool/emesis, and ordered labs.
interventions: Follow sepsis/bleeding response orders and maintain appropriate access/monitoring.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics and reversal strategies are ordered based on the complication; do not independently alter anticoagulants.
teaching: Report fever, shaking chills, jaundice, black stools, vomiting blood, or severe pain urgently.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; sepsis/bleeding interpretation and emergency escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Attributing fever after ERCP to a normal inflammatory response.
oneLinePearl: Post-ERCP fever, shock, or bleeding is never routine recovery.

title: After Paracentesis: Watch Perfusion, Leakage, and Bleeding
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After paracentesis, monitor blood pressure, symptoms, puncture-site leakage/bleeding, abdominal findings, and ordered fluid/laboratory follow-up. Dizziness, hypotension, severe pain, bleeding, or worsening illness requires escalation.
recognize: Persistent leak, new severe abdominal pain, faintness, tachycardia, or hemodynamic change are not simple comfort issues.
priorities: Assess perfusion and puncture site and report significant symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, abdominal symptoms, site drainage, fluid removed as documented, and renal/electrolyte status when ordered.
interventions: Maintain dressing and positioning per protocol and reinforce the prescribed postprocedure plan.
medicationSafety: Albumin or other volume-expansion strategies depend on indication/volume/clinical plan and are not universal nursing-initiated treatment.
teaching: Report dizziness, worsening pain, fever, or persistent drainage from the site.
delegationScope: Routine postprocedure monitoring may be shared; unstable findings require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Assuming every patient automatically needs the same albumin dose after paracentesis.
oneLinePearl: After fluid removal, reassess perfusion—not just abdominal size.

title: PEG Site Problems: Leakage, Pain, or Peritonitis Need More Than Dressing Changes
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: A gastrostomy site should be assessed for secure position, skin integrity, leakage, infection, and feeding tolerance. Severe abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, fever, rapidly increasing leakage, dislodgement, or systemic instability requires immediate escalation before feeding continues.
recognize: New severe pain/distention or formula leaking into tissue can indicate tube displacement or peritoneal complication.
priorities: Stop feeding when serious displacement/peritonitis is suspected and notify the qualified team immediately.
assessMonitor: Check external length/position markers per device plan, site drainage, skin, abdominal findings, temperature, and feeding tolerance.
interventions: Protect skin and maintain securement; do not blindly reinsert a newly dislodged tube outside trained protocol.
medicationSafety: Verify medications are suitable for tube administration and placement is appropriate before use.
teaching: Report sudden tube movement, severe pain, fever, or major leakage promptly.
delegationScope: Routine stoma care may be delegated to trained staff; dislodgement and suspected peritonitis require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Immediately using a dislodged/reinserted tube without placement evaluation.
oneLinePearl: When a PEG moves and the abdomen hurts, stop using it and escalate.

title: Liver Biopsy Aftercare: Bleeding and Referred Shoulder Pain Need Context
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After liver biopsy, monitor hemodynamics, puncture-site bleeding, abdominal pain, and overall condition. Severe/worsening RUQ or shoulder pain, dizziness, hypotension, tachycardia, or increasing abdominal distention may indicate bleeding and requires prompt escalation.
recognize: Some discomfort can occur, but progressive pain plus perfusion change is concerning.
priorities: Assess ABCs/hemodynamics and pain trajectory and notify the procedural team for concerning findings.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, pain, abdominal findings, site bleeding, and ordered labs.
medicationSafety: Medication/anticoagulant restart timing is individualized; avoid NSAIDs or other agents contrary to procedural instructions.
teaching: Seek care for severe pain, dizziness, breathing difficulty, fever, or bleeding after discharge.
delegationScope: Routine postprocedure observations may be shared; signs of internal bleeding require licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Treating increasing shoulder pain with analgesia only while BP is falling.
oneLinePearl: After biopsy, pain plus perfusion change means think bleeding.

title: Endoscopy Discharge: Recovery Is Not Complete Until the Safety Plan Is Clear
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Endoscopy discharge teaching must cover sedation restrictions, medication restart instructions, diet/activity plan, expected minor symptoms, and the specific bleeding, perforation, infection, or pancreatitis warning signs relevant to the procedure.
recognize: Different procedures carry different post-discharge risks; generic 'call if worse' teaching is insufficient.
priorities: Confirm recovery criteria and teach-back of red flags and medication plan before discharge.
assessMonitor: Verify stable vital signs/mental status, pain/nausea control, safe transportation, and understanding of instructions.
interventions: Provide written procedure-specific instructions and contact pathway.
medicationSafety: Clarify anticoagulant/antiplatelet, diabetes, and analgesic restart instructions rather than assuming the preprocedure schedule resumes immediately.
teaching: Use the exact procedure-specific warning signs and transportation restrictions.
delegationScope: PN/LVN may reinforce teaching according to policy; the discharge plan and medication changes require authorized clinical direction.
examTrap: Discharging a sedated patient to drive themselves home because vital signs are normal.
oneLinePearl: A stable recovery bay patient still needs a safe ride, medication plan, and red-flag plan.
